articles.title: Why People Leave: Honour, Fate and Fear at Home
articles.excerpt: Accounts of leaving Islam keep returning to honour, free will and fear at home. Each question is weighed on the sources.
articles.content:
Accounts of leaving Islam keep returning to three questions. What do I owe a family that guards its honour more closely than it guards me? If God wrote everything in advance, what was my choice worth? And what do I do with fear in my own home? None of them is a proof against Islam or for it. Each asks what Islam itself says, and each deserves an answer from the sources.

Where these questions come from

They come from the pattern across many accounts of leaving, not from any one person. This page is built from that pattern alone. It names no one from those accounts, quotes none of them and repeats no private detail. The scholarly works cited are named in the sources.

The first thing to say is that the experience behind these accounts is not in dispute. A child who is hit, shamed and told that their feelings are forbidden has been wronged. No argument below asks anyone to doubt that. The question is whether the wrong came from revelation or from what people built around it.

Honour: whose reputation is being protected?

Many accounts describe a community in which the fault of one becomes the fault of all, and a choice between saving face and protecting a daughter. Readers from many cultures will know that choice.

The Quran sets the measure of a person against it. Humanity is made into peoples and tribes so that they may know one another, and the most honoured with God is the most conscious of Him (49:13). Ismāʿīl al-Fārūqī counted ethnocentrism an offence against divine transcendence, because it sets up a second source of good and evil beside God. A family name that outranks a daughter's safety is such a second source.

Consent in marriage shows the difference between source and custom. Classical jurists did differ on whether a father could contract a first marriage for his daughter without asking her, and the sites should say so. The Prophet's rulings point one way: a woman is not married until she is consulted or gives her permission (al-Bukhārī 5136), and he returned the marriage of a woman whose father had married her against her will (al-Bukhārī 5138). The long answer is in Women, God, and Islamic Law, and on honour in Honour Killings: Culture, Not Islam. Dress and control are weighed in Is the Hijab About Male Control, or Divine Command?

Fate: was any of it my choice?

A question that recurs is what the point of trying can be if God had already settled a person's fate in this life and the next. Teachers often reply that God knows everything and also gave us free will, and leave it there as a bare statement.

It deserves an argument. Knowing is not compelling: that God knows what a person will choose does not make Him the one who chooses. The Quran addresses people as answerable: "let whoever wills believe" (18:29), and the weight of an atom of good or of evil will be seen (99:7-8). Al-Fārūqī reads the trust of 33:72 as the point of the whole creation: nature obeys by necessity, and man alone may obey freely, which is what makes an act moral. Without that freedom, judgement would be meaningless. The full treatment is in If God Knew Everything in Advance, How Is My Choice Genuinely Free?

Fear at home: what does the text allow?

Accounts record violence between parents, and a parent who says that the harm is for the good of those who suffer it. Whoever says that on behalf of Islam should be asked for the text. The article Does Quran 4:34 Permit a Husband to Beat His Wife? weighs the verse on the sources: what the key word means, the sequence the verse sets out, what the earliest authorities permitted and what the Prophet did.

If you are in danger now, contact your local emergency services or a person you trust nearby. Your safety comes before any question on this page.

The demand for consistency

Many who leave hold that a religion should be taken whole or left whole, and they have no patience for those who explain rules away. That demand is fair, and this site accepts it. Reason and revelation come from one source and cannot finally contradict each other. When they seem to, the reader returns to the reading, and revelation itself is not bent.

What follows is a claim that can be tested. The failures these accounts describe sit in the historical form: practices, customs and rulings built around the revelation. The revelation itself says that there is no compulsion in religion (2:256) and that every person answers for their own deeds. A reader who doubts this should test it on the texts, and the articles linked here give the sources to do it. For the doubt itself, see Is Doubt Permitted in Islam? and, for the cost of leaving, Why Can People Not Leave Islam Without Consequences?

If the question is personal

Standing in the same place?

murtadd.org answers doubts with care and without pressure. These pages take the three questions above one at a time:

  • Disappointing my parents
  • Married off without consent
  • If it was all written
  • I was hurt and nobody helped

Frequently asked questions

Do accounts of leaving show that Islam is false?

No. An account records what happened to a person and what they concluded. It can show harm, and it deserves a hearing for that. Whether the harm follows from the revelation or from the customs around it is a question for the texts.

Is family honour an Islamic idea?

The Quran and the Prophet's rulings on consent and on the worth of a person measure people by their conduct and not by their lineage. Honour as the protection of a family's name at a woman's cost belongs to custom, and it appears in many communities that have never been Muslim.

If God knows what I will choose, is my choice real?

Yes. Knowing a choice does not make the choice. The Quran treats people as answerable for what they do, and the linked article sets out the classical and modern answers.

Where can I read from people who have been in the same place?

On murtadd.org, in the pages linked above. You can read without giving your name.

Sources

  • Patterns drawn from public accounts of leaving Islam, kept anonymous and in aggregate. No person, family, place, title or quotation is used.
  • Quran 2:256, 18:29, 33:72, 49:13 and 99:7-8, cited by reference.
  • Al-Bukhārī 5136 and 5138, on consent in marriage, as cited in the murtadd.org page Married off without consent.
  • Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life (International Institute of Islamic Thought, 2nd ed., 1992), on ethnocentrism and on the trust of 33:72.

articles.title: Which Old Testament Does the Islamic Dilemma Mean?
articles.excerpt: Jews, Protestants, Catholics, the Orthodox and the Ethiopian church count the Old Testament differently. What each list is, and who fixed it.
articles.content:
The Islamic dilemma speaks of "the Torah" as if one Old Testament lay in every hand. Jews, Protestants, Catholics, the Orthodox and the Ethiopian church count the books differently, and each count has its own history.

The Hebrew list

Josephus, writing in the first century, counted twenty-two books "which are justly believed to be divine" (Davidson, p. 28). Davidson, writing in 1877, called Josephus an authority of small weight whose statement was "probably expressed in exaggerated terms" (p. 39). No council fixed this list. The rabbis debated particular books such as Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, and the sources do not record a vote on a list.

The Greek list

The Greek Old Testament of the churches carries more books than the Hebrew list. In the Vatican manuscript they stand among the others: Tobit and Judith between Nehemiah and Esther, Wisdom and Sirach after the Song of Songs, Baruch after Jeremiah, and three books of Maccabees at the close (p. 47). Davidson wrote that "The very way in which apocryphal are inserted among canonical books in the Alexandrian canon, shows the equal rank assigned to both" (p. 47). Later scholars doubt that a closed Alexandrian canon ever existed, since the great Greek codices are Christian manuscripts of the fourth century and later.

The Catholic list

"The Roman Catholic canon was finally determined at the Council of Trent (1546), which adopted all the books in the Vulgate as sacred and canonical, without distinction" (p. 123). Trent left out 3 and 4 Esdras, 3 Maccabees and the Prayer of Manasseh. The Vatican Council of 1870 confirmed the decree (p. 123).

The Protestant list

The Reformers returned to the Hebrew Old Testament and called the other books apocryphal, though useful (pp. 108 to 110). The Second Helvetic Confession of 1566 says they may be read in church but do not bind in matters of faith (p. 121). The Westminster Confession denies that they are inspired or part of the canon (p. 123).

The Orthodox list

The Greek church kept the older distinction until the seventeenth century. Davidson records that it canonised the apocryphal books at a synod in Jerusalem under Dositheus in 1672: "This was done at a Jerusalem synod under Dositheus in 1672" (p. 124).

The Ethiopian list

The Ethiopian canon was fluctuating. Davidson reports that it at first held all the Greek books together with Enoch, 4 Esdras and Jubilees, and that later lists vary (pp. 104 to 105). The letter of Jude quotes Enoch (p. 52).

What this means for the Islamic dilemma

The Quran names the Torah that God gave to Moses and gives no list of books. A premise that treats "the Torah" as one fixed Old Testament has to say which of these lists it means, and when that list was fixed. The Muslim answer in the article on the Islamic dilemma does not need to settle the question. It needs only to show that the question has no single answer.

Sources

  • Samuel Davidson, The Canon of the Bible: Its Formation, History, and Fluctuations (New York: Peter Eckler, 1877; Project Gutenberg eBook 30132), pp. 28, 39, 47, 52, 104 to 105, 108 to 110, 121 and 123 to 124.
  • Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (Minneapolis: Fortress, 2012); John Barton, Holy Writings, Sacred Text: The Canon in Early Christianity (Louisville: Westminster John Knox, 1997); Roger T. Beckwith, The Old Testament Canon of the New Testament Church (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1985).
  • Albert C. Sundberg, The Old Testament of the Early Church (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1964), on the Greek codices.

faq.q: Do Jews, Catholics and Protestants count the same Old Testament books?
faq.a: No. Jews and Protestants share the books of the Hebrew list, which Protestants arrange differently. The Catholic list follows the Vulgate, as Trent confirmed in 1546, and carries more books. The Orthodox and Ethiopian lists carry more again.

faq.q: Did a council decide the Old Testament canon?
faq.a: No single council decided it for all. Trent decided for the Catholic Church in 1546, and a synod at Jerusalem decided for the Greek church in 1672. The Hebrew list came about without a vote that the sources record.

faq.q: Which Old Testament does the Quran mean by the Torah?
faq.a: The Quran speaks of the Torah that God gave to Moses and names no list of books. Muslim scholars discuss what of it survives. This article does not decide that question.
